intro: All eight trees here stand inside one gate. Spring Grove Cemetery and Arboretum, founded in 1845, keeps a run of Ohio state champions, each marked by a small boulder and sign, and one of them is the largest September elm known in the country. A yellow buckeye older than the cemetery survives from the Mill Creek floodplain. A dawn redwood from the 1948 seed stands beside a cedar of Lebanon raised from 1930 cuttings, and a hardy rubber tree and a katsura share one stop in Section 53.
meta_description: Eight champion trees in Cincinnati's Spring Grove Cemetery: a yellow buckeye older than the cemetery and the largest known September elm in the US.
question_meta: Cincinnati's oldest tree on this map is a yellow buckeye at Spring Grove Cemetery, older than the cemetery's founding in 1845.
question_answer: The oldest tree on our Cincinnati map is the yellow buckeye in Section 22 of Spring Grove Cemetery and Arboretum, at 4521 Spring Grove Ave. The cemetery was founded in 1845 and says this tree was already standing.
question_context: Nobody has published a closer date, so older than the cemetery is the whole of what can be said, and it is a good deal. Spring Grove describes the buckeye as a survivor of the Mill Creek floodplain community of yellow buckeye, American elm and sycamore that grew here before the grounds were laid out. It is also the Ohio state champion of its species, 452 centimetres round and 31.7 metres tall on the state register. Most of the other champions at Spring Grove have younger, better documented origins. The dawn redwood in Section 18 came from the seed distributed in 1948, after the species was found alive in China. The cedar of Lebanon beside it descends from 19 cuttings sent by the Arnold Arboretum in 1930, after the cemetery's first cedar died of the cold. The bald cypress near the Fleischmann Mausoleum, 120 metres from the buckeye, has the largest girth of the eight at 538 centimetres, and its age has never been published. Each champion carries a small boulder with a State Champion sign, and the map is available from the Customer Service Center.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Cincinnati?
faq.a: On this map it is the yellow buckeye in Section 22 of Spring Grove Cemetery. The cemetery was founded in 1845 and says the tree predates it. No closer date has been published.

faq.q: How do you find the champion trees at Spring Grove?
faq.a: Each one is marked by a small boulder with a State Champion sign. The Customer Service Center has a free self-guided map, and cars may drive the grounds.

faq.q: Is it free to visit Spring Grove's trees?
faq.a: Visitor listings say entry and parking are free, and the grounds open daily from 8am to 6pm, until 8pm on Monday and Thursday from May through August. It is an active cemetery, so stay on the roads and paths.

faq.q: Why is a dawn redwood at Spring Grove so special?
faq.a: The species was known only from fossils until living trees were found in China in the 1940s. Spring Grove's Ohio champion comes from the first seed distributed in 1948, and it is already 505 centimetres round.

trees.name: September Elm (national champion)

location.address: Spring Grove Cemetery and Arboretum, 4521 Spring Grove Ave, Cincinnati, OH 45232

trees.story:
The largest September elm known in the United States grows among the graves of a Cincinnati cemetery. American Forests has carried it on the national register since 2018, and Ohio lists it as state champion as well.

The numbers are modest for a record holder. In 2013 it measured 93 inches round, 236 centimetres, and 94 feet tall, 28.7 metres, with a crown 56 feet across. September elm is a rare native of the south-central United States and, as the name suggests, it flowers late in the year.

In August 2025 Spring Grove's horticulture director told the Cincinnati Enquirer that the arboretum still lists it under both titles and that it is due to be measured again, so the figures here may already be behind the tree.

Spring Grove has been a cemetery since 1845 and is an arboretum too, with its champions spread across the grounds and each one marked by a small boulder and a State Champion sign. Its own page gives no section number for this elm, and the pin comes from the state register, so it is close rather than exact. The Customer Service Center has the map.

Nobody has published when this tree started. If you know, tell us.

trees.name: Bald Cypress by the Fleischmann Mausoleum

location.address: Spring Grove Cemetery, Section 20 near the Fleischmann Mausoleum, Cincinnati, OH 45232

trees.story:
The trunk of Ohio's champion bald cypress is so deeply fissured that measuring it is a problem in itself. The state register settles on 212 inches, 538 centimetres, and the folds in the wood make that figure closer to a negotiated settlement than a reading.

Above that waist the tree climbs 113 feet, 34.4 metres, under a crown 61 feet wide. It scores 340 points on the champion formula, and it stands in Section 20 of Spring Grove, across the road from Cedar Lake and close to the Fleischmann Mausoleum.

The species has a habit of sending woody knees up from its roots, and the tallest at Spring Grove rise around Cedar Lake in Section 21, just over the road.

There is a temptation here worth resisting. Spring Grove also has a Baldcypress Grove planted in the 1880s, but that is a different place on the grounds and nothing ties this tree to it. Its age has not been published anywhere we can find. If you know when it went in, tell us.

A small boulder with a State Champion sign marks it, and the champion yellow buckeye, older than the cemetery itself, stands about 120 metres away.

trees.name: Pre-cemetery Yellow Buckeye

location.address: Spring Grove Cemetery, Section 22, Cincinnati, OH 45232

trees.story:
This buckeye was here first. Spring Grove Cemetery was founded in 1845, and its own arboretum says the tree is older than that, a survivor of the woods that once covered the floodplain of Mill Creek, where yellow buckeye grew alongside American elm and sycamore.

So the cemetery came to the tree. Every founder, family and funeral in the place's history arrived after it did. Nobody has published how much older than 1845 it is, and we will not guess.

The state register has it at 178 inches round, 452 centimetres, and 104 feet tall, 31.7 metres, with a crown 77 feet across. That makes it Ohio's champion yellow buckeye, on 301 points. Yellow buckeye is native along the Ohio River, so the species is no surprise here. The size is.

Like every champion at Spring Grove it has a small boulder with a State Champion sign. The pin comes from the state register and is close rather than exact. The champion bald cypress stands about 120 metres away, near the Fleischmann Mausoleum in Section 20.

trees.name: Dawn Redwood from the 1948 seed

location.address: Spring Grove Cemetery, Section 18 by Willow Water Lake, Cincinnati, OH 45232

trees.story:
Scientists knew this species from fossils before anyone knew it was still alive. Then, in the 1940s, living dawn redwoods turned up in China, and the Arnold Arboretum funded an expedition to collect seed. It went out to gardens in 1948, and Spring Grove's champion comes from that first distribution.

Which means this tree is under eighty years old and already 199 inches round, 505 centimetres. It stands 94 feet tall, 28.7 metres, with a crown 51 feet across, and the state register gives it 305 points and the Ohio title. For a state champion that is very little time.

Nobody has published the year this particular seedling went into the ground, so 1948 is the earliest it could have been rather than the date it was.

It stands in Section 18, along the road west of Willow Water Lake, with the state champion cedar of Lebanon right beside it. That cedar arrived from the same arboretum, eighteen years earlier, for a very different reason. The champion lacebark pine is about 110 metres away, behind the waterfall. Each is marked by a small boulder and a State Champion sign, and the pin comes from the state register, so it is close rather than exact.

trees.name: Cedar of Lebanon from the 1930 cuttings

location.address: Spring Grove Cemetery, Section 18 west of Willow Water Lake, Cincinnati, OH 45232

trees.story:
The first cedar of Lebanon planted at Spring Grove died of the cold. It was not hardy enough for Ohio. So in 1930 the Arnold Arboretum sent 19 cuttings taken from trees at the northern end of the species' range, in the Taurus Mountains, where the winters had already done the selecting.

This tree is from that stock, and it is now the state champion. The Ohio register gives 124 inches round, 315 centimetres, and 66 feet tall, 20.1 metres, with a crown 46 feet across and 201 points. Spring Grove's own page has it slightly smaller, at 122 inches, 64 feet and 197 points, which looks like an earlier measure of the same tree.

The year this one went into the ground has not been published. It belongs to the 1930 stock, and that is as close as anyone has said.

Its neighbour along the road west of Willow Water Lake, in Section 18, is the champion dawn redwood, a species that arrived in the same grounds by way of the same arboretum. The state register's own coordinate for this cedar lies about 480 metres from where Spring Grove says it stands, so the pin follows Spring Grove and is approximate. Look for the small boulder and State Champion sign.

trees.name: Katsura champion in Section 53

location.address: Spring Grove Cemetery, Section 53, Cincinnati, OH 45232

trees.story:
Spring Grove has held Ohio's katsura title twice, with two different trees. The original champion stands at the north tip of Section 22. It lost the crown. This one, in Section 53, then took it back for the cemetery, and it is the tree the state register lists today.

The register gives 180 inches round, 457 centimetres, and 78 feet tall, 23.8 metres, with a crown 67 feet wide and 274 points. It grows with several leaders rather than one straight stem, so do not expect a single clean column. Round a multi-leader tree, the tape is measuring something more complicated than a trunk.

Spring Grove says it is not quite as old as 1865, the year the species was introduced to cultivation, and that is the only clue to its age anyone has offered. No planting date has been published. If you have one, tell us.

It stands about 35 metres from the state champion hardy rubber tree, so the two make one stop. A small boulder with a State Champion sign marks it, and the pin comes from the register, so it is close rather than exact.

trees.name: Hardy Rubber Tree by the shelter house

location.address: Spring Grove Cemetery, Section 53 west of the shelter house, Cincinnati, OH 45232

trees.story:
The hardy rubber tree holds up to 3 percent latex and nobody uses it for rubber. The latex shows when a leaf or a seed capsule splits, fine evidence of a talent the tree has never been asked to use.

This one is Ohio's champion. The state register has it at 130 inches round, 330 centimetres, and just 60 feet tall, 18.3 metres. The crown is wider than the tree is high by either count, 67 feet on Spring Grove's page and 83 in the register, and you can walk in beneath it and stand under the whole canopy. Seedlings come up in its shade.

The IUCN lists the species as Vulnerable, which gives a state champion in an Ohio cemetery a certain extra interest. Nobody has published when it was planted. If you know, tell us.

It stands west of the shelter house in Section 53, about 35 metres from the champion katsura, and carries the small boulder and State Champion sign used across Spring Grove. The pin comes from the state register, so it is close rather than exact. Its name promises an industry that never came to it.

trees.name: Lacebark Pine behind the waterfall

location.address: Spring Grove Cemetery, Section 18 by the waterfall, Cincinnati, OH 45232

trees.story:
Ohio's champion lacebark pine is only 152 centimetres round, and it does not need to be any bigger. The bark comes off in a patchwork of white, olive, purple and silver, so the trunk looks assembled from several other trees.

The figures are small for a state title: 60 inches round, 54 feet tall, 16.5 metres, a crown 25 feet across, 120 points in all. The champion dawn redwood, about 110 metres away, scores 305. Nobody comes to this one for the tape measure.

Its site was chosen. Spring Grove says the pine was planted at a place with special meaning, beside the lot of the Rowe family, whose name is on the Rowe Arboretum, and a large carved Celtic cross stands near it. The tree sits behind the waterfall in Section 18, and you can see it easily from the road above.

Nobody has published when it went in. If you know, tell us.

Like the other champions it has a small boulder with a State Champion sign, and the pin comes from the state register, so it is close rather than exact. Take the road above the waterfall and look down.
